source.title: Prescriptive Scaling Laws for Data Constrained Training
source.authors: Justin Lovelace; Christian K. Belardi; Srivatsa Kundurthy; S. Sudhakar; K. Weinberger

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present
record.tranche_reason: The study refines data-constrained scaling laws and reports that existing laws miss loss increases under repetition. It also shows that fitting and training choices can change fit quality and compute-optimal allocation.
record.gate_note: The study directly measures validation loss across parameter counts, unique-token budgets, and repetition levels; fits and compares scaling laws; and evaluates configurations recommended at fixed compute budgets. It also reports downstream BPB, but does not test a relationship between downstream performance and scale or pretraining loss. Referenced results from other studies are not recorded as findings here.
record.test_reason: The study trains 300+ Llama-2-style models (15M–1B params, 50M–6B unique tokens, up to 16 epochs) and fits Chinchilla and repetition laws. It shows that existing laws underpredict loss under heavy repetition, that a Chinchilla allocation is beaten in data-constrained settings, and that baseline refitting and weight decay change fitted parameters and allocation advice.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also state that the Chinchilla law and the effective-data laws systematically underpredict loss under heavy repetition. Their law predicts a compute threshold beyond which further repetition is counterproductive and model size should grow instead. They trace the disagreement with Muennighoff et al. to a poorly fitting transferred Chinchilla baseline.
record.recipe_differences: The paper retains a Chinchilla-style single-epoch base but adds an explicit repetition-dependent overfitting penalty, in one-, two-, and four-parameter forms; it also tests weight decay and prescriptive allocations.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome and fitted form depend on repetition level, model capacity relative to unique data, weight decay (λ = 0.1 versus 1.0), and whether the Chinchilla baseline is refit on the relevant runs. The compute-optimal allocation direction changes when the transferred baseline is refit.

fits_no_version.finding: Strong weight decay cuts the fitted overfitting coefficient P by about 70% and produces a predicted crossover at about 3.2e18 FLOPs.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Regularization strength modulates the repetition penalty in data-constrained scaling laws.

fits_no_version.finding: Downstream OLMES BPB is best for the additive-penalty recommendations in Table 1 and mixed in Table 2.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Configurations recommended by the loss law also tend to give the best aggregate downstream BPB. This is not a predictability test.

record.problems: The study's own model sizes reach 1B parameters and repetition reaches 16 epochs; the authors state they cannot confirm the fitted exponents at frontier scales or beyond the tested repetition range. Only two weight-decay values are tested. Fits use Huber loss in log-space and bootstrap MAD is reported for fitted parameters, but the paper does not provide uncertainty for the prescriptive validation outcomes.
record.rows_left_out: Per-task BPB breakdowns in Appendix E, Tables 17–21, are omitted because aggregate BPB comparisons are recorded and the per-task results do not test the downstream-predictability version. Figure-only allocation-frontier details are summarized in the paper's explicit text rather than transcribed as additional rows.

untested.parts: Scales beyond about 1B parameters and 6B tokens; the range covers about two orders of magnitude in N. Kaplan-style compute scaling is not tested.
No numerical loss extrapolation is checked against much larger runs. Prescriptive validation compares configuration rankings only.
No stable power-law exponent for optimal N and D against compute is estimated. The Kaplan-versus-Hoffmann split is not tested in the unconstrained regime.
Depth and width are not varied at fixed parameter count.
Other modalities, fine-tuning and transfer are not tested; only repeated-data pretraining is.
Downstream BPB is reported for chosen configurations, but its predictability from scale or loss is not tested.

missing.what: Fitted Chinchilla exponents differ by setup: α 0.300 / β 0.427 at λ=0.1, α 0.292 / β 0.533 at λ=1.0, and α 0.336 / β 0.387 on Muennighoff C4.
Single-epoch compute-optimal allocation shifts toward larger models under strong weight decay, with a loss premium at every compute budget.
Optimum at 1e22 FLOPs and 25B unique tokens: published Chinchilla gives 9.2B/7ep, refit Chinchilla gives 5.7B/12ep; published D,N gives 7.0B/9ep, refit D,N gives 6.3B/11ep.
The published-base D,N fit has R*_N=5.31, while the refit base has R*_N=3,294, which effectively disables the N mechanism.

record.verdict_notes: V5's 'repeated data' regime is directly tested; the record wrongly marked V5 as not tested. The Table 2 weight-decay rows were mislinked to V3: they compare regularization settings, not allocation exponents. Rows R8, R9, R12, R13, R15 and R16 are the study's own-method fits and bear on V5 only as evidence that a modified power-law form fits. The validation models (2.2B, 3B, 5B) exceed the fit range, but only rankings are compared, so V2 is untested.

versions.untested_parts: The study fits a Chinchilla power law on single-epoch runs and evaluates repetition-augmented laws, but does not test all training regimes or scales beyond its stated ranges.
No explicit test fits a law only on small runs and compares numerical loss predictions with runs orders of magnitude larger.

The study evaluates allocations for fixed compute and unique-data budgets in data-constrained, repeated-data settings; it does not estimate or establish a general power-law exponent for optimal parameter and token counts across compute.
Architecture depth, width, and other architecture details are not varied to test their effect at fixed parameter count.
No other modality, fine-tuning, transfer, or other training regime is tested.
Downstream BPB is reported for selected configurations, but its relationship to pretraining loss or scale is not tested for predictability.

The study tests dependence on repetition, weight decay, baseline fitting, and fitting method within the reported model and data ranges; it does not test every possible parameter-counting, schedule, or dataset choice.

source_check.condition: Data-constrained budgets (250M–500M unique tokens) requiring repetition
source_check.reason: Table 1 shows larger, fewer-epoch configurations beating Chinchilla recommendations at all three budgets. This qualifies extending that allocation to repeated-data settings.

relationships.condition: Multi-epoch (repeated-data) pretraining up to 16 epochs (64 on the C4 data)
relationships.reason: Neither the plain token power law nor the effective-data forms capture the loss rise under repetition (R3, R4, R6, R7, R14). A power law in repetition count has to be added (R5, R8, R9, R15, R16).
relationships.display_finding: Plain token and effective-data laws failed to capture rising loss under repetition, requiring an additional power law in repetition.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.condition: Multi-epoch (repeated-data) pretraining up to 16 epochs (64 on the C4 data)
source_check.reason: The original and effective-data forms miss high-repetition loss increases; adding a repetition-dependent penalty improves fits on FineWeb and C4. The broader repeated-data regime therefore requires a qualified form.

relationships.condition: Choice of law form, weight decay setting, and whether the Chinchilla baseline is refit
relationships.reason: Refitting the baseline lifts single-epoch R² from 0.711 to 0.989 and reverses the allocation (R17, R18). Weight decay shifts the fitted E, B and β and the penalty exponents (R2, R13). Prior-law R² swings from 0.58 to 0.95 with weight decay (R6, R10, R11). Optimal configurations differ by weight decay (R43, R47, R55).
relationships.display_finding: Refitting the baseline increased single-epoch R² from 0.711 to 0.989 and reversed allocation; weight decay changed E, B, β, penalty exponents, and optimal configurations, while prior-law R² ranged from 0.58 to 0.95 across weight-decay settings.
